cards.title: Polynomial testing of induced four-cycle freeness
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that the canonical sampling test below, with sample size \[s(\varepsilon)=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil,\] rejects every finite simple graph that is \(\varepsilon\)-far from having no induced four-cycle with probability at least \(2/3\), for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\)? The constants must be independent of the graph order and of \(\varepsilon\). The test always accepts graphs with no induced four-cycle, so this asks for polynomial-query one-sided testing in the dense graph model.
cards.why: This is the unresolved concrete case, up to complementation, in the classification of polynomial testing for a single forbidden induced graph. It asks whether a globally expensive repair necessarily leaves violations visible in a polynomial-sized random sample. The answer would separate two very different quantitative regimes of dense-graph testing for one small and fully specified pattern.
cards.status_note: Source-open as Conjecture 3.6 in the 23 August 2025 survey and in the paragraph after Theorem 1.1 of the checked Gishboliner–Shapira author manuscript. A bounded review on 15 September 2026 checked the original theorem, publication metadata and the August 2026 quantitative container characterization, without finding a polynomial bound or a refutation for the selected case. The new target was explicitly authorized by the user and is not asserted equivalent to the inherited general classification programme. Source proofs have not been independently verified or formalized in Lean.

progress.text: Alon–Fox prove polynomial testability for cographs, the graphs with no induced four-vertex path, and identify induced four-cycle freeness as the remaining single-pattern case up to complementation.

Goldreich poses the general polynomial-query classification question as Open Problem 8.26. This is the inherited source direction; the present concrete target was chosen later with explicit user authorization.

Gishboliner–Shapira's Theorem 1.1 proves that a graph far from induced-four-cycle freeness contains at least \(n^{4}/2^{(1/\varepsilon)^{c}}\) induced copies for an absolute constant \(c\), under their distance convention. The paragraph immediately following the theorem conjectures a polynomial improvement. The May 2018 author revision and the 2019 journal publication are distinguished.
The Polynomial Property Testing survey explicitly restates the polynomial induced-four-cycle conjecture as Conjecture 3.6, alongside the almost complete single-pattern classification in Theorem 3.5.

Carenini–Seth–Yoshida give a quantitative container characterization of size-oblivious one-sided testing. The checked Theorem 1.4 and Corollary 1.7 do not establish the polynomial bound for this specific induced pattern.

sentences: The question asks whether induced four-cycle freeness can be tested from a random sample whose size is polynomial in reciprocal proximity.
An induced four-cycle has its four cycle edges and neither diagonal, and repairing the graph permits both edge additions and deletions.
The canonical tester rejects when its sampled induced subgraph contains such a cycle and must reject every far graph with probability at least two thirds.
An exponential removal bound is known, while the polynomial improvement remains explicitly conjectured in the checked 2025 source.
This concrete target was selected with user authorization from the broader inherited classification question and would settle its remaining single-pattern case up to complementation.

cards.definitions: A finite simple graph is an undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), where \(n\ge1\), \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(E\) is a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. An induced four-cycle consists of four distinct vertices \(v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\) whose edges among those vertices are exactly \(\{v_1,v_2\},\{v_2,v_3\},\{v_3,v_4\},\{v_4,v_1\}\); the two diagonals are absent. Let \(\mathcal P_n\) be the graphs on \([n]\) with no such induced subgraph. Define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\min_{([n],E')\in\mathcal P_n}|E\mathbin{\triangle}E'|.\] Here \(\triangle\) is symmetric difference, so both edge additions and deletions are allowed and each undirected edit is counted once. The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. The graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far when \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)>\varepsilon\), with strict inequality. This uses the edge-count-over-\(n^{2}\) convention of the selected survey; it is half the adjacency-matrix-entry distance in the original Goldreich question. The tester is given \(n\) and rational \(\varepsilon\), and has oracle access to the adjacency bit of any unordered vertex pair. For a positive integer \(s\), the canonical test chooses a uniformly random subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of cardinality \(\min\{n,s\}\), queries every unordered pair in \(S\), and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced four-cycle. All \(\binom{\min\{n,s\}}{2}\) adjacency queries count; the property check on the finite sampled graph has no additional query cost, and no running-time bound is requested. Uniform subset sampling is the stated finite probability distribution, with sampling and local computation not charged as adjacency queries. If \(n\le s\), the entire graph is inspected. In particular, orders below four are always accepted and never far. No behavior is required for nonsatisfying graphs at distance at most \(\varepsilon\). Every host graph is allowed; no degree, density, chordality or other promise is imposed. The deterministic sampling-size formula and rejection rule specify a single uniform family of tests once \(C,a\) are fixed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the formal proposition or its logical negation with a complete Lean-checked proof. A positive answer must exhibit fixed polynomial constants and establish rejection probability at least \(2/3\) for every far input and every permitted proximity parameter. A negative answer must show that for every choice of \(C,a\) there are a proximity parameter and a graph at the stated distance for which that sampling test rejects with probability less than \(2/3\). A merely exponential sample bound, a result for ordinary four-cycle freeness, or a tester with an additional host-graph promise does not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: An induced four-cycle is a cycle without either diagonal. A complete graph on four vertices contains ordinary four-cycles, but no induced four-cycle. This distinction changes both the set of valid graphs and the repair task: adding a diagonal can destroy an induced cycle, while adding edges cannot eliminate an ordinary subgraph copy.

The tester does not try to find every violation or to reconstruct a repaired graph. It distinguishes graphs satisfying the property from graphs requiring more than \(\varepsilon n^{2}\) edits. A polynomial sample bound would mean that the number of queried adjacencies remains polynomial in reciprocal proximity even when the host graph is arbitrarily large.

The induced removal lemma relates edit distance to the number of forbidden induced copies. For a fixed pattern, polynomial bounds on that density and polynomial bounds for canonical one-sided sampling are equivalent up to changes in polynomial exponents. The known four-cycle removal bound is exponential in a power of reciprocal distance, which is far larger than the polynomial dependence conjectured here.

Alon and Shapira classified the polynomial and superpolynomial cases for single forbidden induced graphs apart from a few small patterns. Alon and Fox settled the four-vertex-path case, leaving the induced four-cycle and its complement as the remaining case. Complementing all adjacencies preserves edit distance and transfers the sampling question between those two patterns.

On 15 September 2026 the user authorized replacing the inherited classification programme by a concrete narrower statement. The selected target is Conjecture 3.6 of the 2025 survey. Goldreich's Open Problem 8.26 concerns all dense-graph properties, permits two-sided error, and asks for a characterization; it is strictly broader in scope and is not asserted equivalent to this testability conjecture. The separate active finite-family classification card also remains a different target.

The 2026 container characterization connects one-sided tester complexity to quantitative combinatorial parameters. It supplies an equivalence, rather than polynomial values of those parameters for every particular property. Consequently, the existence of that characterization does not itself settle the induced-four-cycle bound.

cards.title: Sharp graph-removal bounds for fixed patterns
cards.formal: Determine the asymptotic order of the extremal copy-count function \(M_H(\varepsilon,n)\) defined below, for every fixed connected finite simple graph \(H\) with at least two edges. Both the proximity parameter \(\varepsilon\) and the graph order \(n\) vary. The requested precision is matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants depending only on \(H\), uniformly over all feasible pairs \((\varepsilon,n)\). Thus the answer must specify bounds \(B_H(\varepsilon,n)>0\) and prove that, for each such \(H\), there are constants \(0<c_H\le C_H<\infty\) such that \[c_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\le M_H(\varepsilon,n)\le C_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\] for every feasible pair. The copies are ordinary subgraphs, with extra edges allowed.
cards.why: Removal bounds quantify how visible a forbidden configuration must become once a graph is globally far from avoiding it. Their dependence on the distance parameter controls the sampling cost of detecting violations and connects dense-graph testing to extremal and additive combinatorics. Distinguishing polynomial from superpolynomial dependence identifies a broad boundary, but does not determine the rate on either side of it.
cards.status_note: The source poses this quantitative target in 2017. The source definitions, Fox’s logarithmic-height tower bound, the minimum-degree restriction in Fox–Wigderson, the 2025 survey and the 2025 hypergraph classification were checked on 15 September 2026. A bounded search of later work did not identify matching general bounds; this is not an exhaustive certification of openness or an independent verification of the cited proofs. Constant-factor precision, the subset-copy convention and the feasible-domain treatment are recorded editorial specifications.

progress.text: The graph-removal theorem supplies a positive density guarantee, while the ordinary subgraph-freeness dichotomy distinguishes bipartite patterns, which have polynomial bounds, from nonbipartite patterns, which do not. This is a classification of the broad rate regime, not matching bounds for every pattern.

Fox's Theorem 1 improves the general removal guarantee to an inverse tower of twos whose height is \(O_H(\log(1/\varepsilon))\), after translating distance and copy conventions. This is an upper bound on the required reciprocal density; it is not a matching construction showing that tower growth is necessary.
Goldreich poses the connected-pattern copy-count question as Open Problem 8.17 and summarizes available bounds in Theorem 8.18; footnote 41 records the logarithmic-height tower improvement.

Fox–Wigderson prove linear clique-removal bounds under a minimum degree greater than \((2r-5)n/(2r-3)\) by a fixed positive fraction of \(n\), for the pattern \(K_r\). Below that threshold they recover superpolynomial behavior. The additional minimum-degree hypothesis is absent from the general target.

Gishboliner–Shapira settle the higher-uniformity analogue of the polynomial-removal classification: ordinary hypergraph removal has polynomial bounds precisely for partite patterns. That result does not give matching growth bounds for the nonbipartite graph cases here.

The Polynomial Property Testing survey retains the polynomial/nonpolynomial dichotomy in Section 3.1. A bounded later-work search on 15 September 2026 did not identify matching general bounds for the full copy-count target.

cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(t=|V(H)|\). All graphs are undirected and have neither loops nor multiple edges. A graph is \(H\)-free if there is no injective map \(\phi:V(H)\to V(G)\) taking every edge of \(H\) to an edge of \(G\); nonedges of \(H\) impose no restriction. Let \(r_H(G)\) be the least number of edges that must be deleted from \(G\) to make it \(H\)-free. Allowing edge additions as well cannot decrease this minimum. Use the source's adjacency-matrix distance \(d_H(G)=2r_H(G)/n^{2}\): each changed undirected edge changes two matrix entries. Say that \(G\) is \(\varepsilon\)-far when \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\), with a strict inequality. Define \(N_H(G)\) to be the number of \(t\)-element subsets \(S\subseteq[n]\) for which \(G[S]\) contains an ordinary copy of \(H\), counting each such subset once even if it supports several embeddings. This fixes the copy convention suggested by the source's random-subset test; counting injective labelled embeddings instead changes the count by factors between one and \(t!\). A feasible pair is a rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and an integer \(n\ge t\) for which at least one graph on \([n]\) has \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\). On precisely this domain, set \[M_H(\varepsilon,n)=\min\{N_H(G):V(G)=[n],\ d_H(G)>\varepsilon\}.\] The minimum is over a nonempty finite set, so it is a positive integer. No value is requested for an infeasible pair. The constants in the matching bounds may depend on the whole fixed pattern \(H\), but not on \(n\) or \(\varepsilon\); in particular, \(\varepsilon\) may decrease with \(n\). The target is the growth of this extremal function, not the running time of enumerating graphs. No extra minimum-degree, regularity, randomness or sparsity promise is imposed on \(G\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply the matching asymptotic bounds in the formal statement and a complete Lean-checked proof of both inequalities for every permitted pattern and feasible parameter pair. The lower inequality must hold for every graph at the stated distance, and the upper inequality must establish existence of graphs with the claimed copy count. Merely restating the defining minimization, tabulating finitely many values, giving one-sided bounds, or establishing only that some positive removal bound exists does not meet this growth target. The precision here is a multiplicative constant factor depending only on the pattern, not additive \(1/100\) accuracy on a normalized copy density.

context_blocks.text: For a fixed pattern on \(t\) vertices, a random \(t\)-vertex subset detects a violation with probability exactly \(N_H(G)/\binom{n}{t}\). The extremal function asks how small that probability can be while repairing the whole graph still requires changing a positive fraction of its adjacency matrix. This connects a global repair requirement to the frequency of small observable witnesses.

Ordinary and induced removal are different questions. An ordinary copy only requires the pattern's edges to be present; an induced copy also requires its nonedges to remain absent. For example, three mutually adjacent vertices contain a three-vertex path as an ordinary subgraph, but not as an induced path. This card retains ordinary copies from Definition 8.16 and the connected-pattern scope of Open Problem 8.17.

The classical removal lemma ensures a positive copy density for every fixed positive distance, uniformly over graph order. Its quantitative content can nevertheless be extremely weak: the known general lower guarantee involves an inverse tower of exponentials, while nonbipartite examples exclude every fixed polynomial dependence on distance. A positive constant for each fixed distance therefore says much less than a sharp answer as the distance tends to zero.

The source asks for relatively tight bounds on a function of both distance and graph order. This card makes that precision explicit as constant-factor matching bounds with pattern-dependent constants, retaining both parameters and specifying the feasible domain. It does not silently replace the question by the triangle-only case, by a large-graph limit, or by the already known polynomial/nonpolynomial classification. The matrix normalization differs by a factor of two from the edge-count-over-\(n^{2}\) convention in several later papers.

The dependence on the host graph matters. A sufficiently large minimum degree can give linear removal bounds for cliques, whereas unrestricted hosts admit much smaller copy densities. Such a theorem clarifies a special regime and cannot supply a bound for every graph in the domain of this card.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
